vignette:
Sarah presents as a meticulously composed woman, the kind of person you’d expect to thrive in the high-stakes world of stock brokerage. Her posture is straight, her language precise. But as she speaks, a tremor in her hand betrays the story her body is holding. Three years ago, she was at the top of her game, celebrated for her sharp instincts and an almost preternatural ability to stay calm under pressure. That was before Mark.

The relationship had been intense but short-lived. When she ended it, he didn’t argue. He just started… appearing. First, it was emails, dozens a day, chronicling his love and despair. Then, he was across the street from her office building, just watching. She’d leave a client meeting and find him standing by the coffee cart in the lobby. He never approached, never spoke. He just made sure she saw him. The police said they couldn’t do anything; he wasn’t technically threatening her.

The fear began as a low hum, a background static to her life. She started taking different routes to work, parking in different sections of the garage. The turning point came when she found a small, exquisitely carved wooden bird on her apartment doorstep. It was a replica of a trinket she kept on her desk at work, a gift from her late grandmother. The message was clear: *I can get to you anywhere*. That night, she slept with a chair wedged under her doorknob for the first time.

After a grueling legal process, she secured a restraining order. Mark disappeared. But the feeling of being watched did not.

Now, at 38, Sarah’s world has shrunk to the size of her fear. Her job, once a source of pride and stimulation, has become a minefield. The constant ping of notifications on her trading terminal makes her flinch. She finds herself scanning the faces of new clients, her heart seizing if a name sounds remotely like his. She describes her focus as a pane of glass that’s been shattered; she can see the pieces of the market, the data points and trends, but she can no longer assemble them into a coherent whole. More than once, she has frozen mid-trade, overwhelmed by a sudden, vivid image of his face in a crowd.

Her home is no longer a sanctuary but a fortress. She lives on the 15th floor, yet she checks the locks on her windows every night. She has blackout curtains in every room and keeps them drawn. Her partner, Alex, is patient and kind, but she sees the confusion in his eyes. When he comes home unexpectedly with flowers, her first thought isn't of love, but of intrusion. "How did you get in?" she’ll ask, her voice sharp, before catching herself. She hasn't told him the full story, ashamed of the details, feeling as though she is somehow contaminated by the experience. Her parents, who immigrated to provide a life of stability and success, don't understand. "He is gone," her mother tells her, "You are strong. You must move forward now."

Sleep offers little respite. She is plagued by nightmares where she is running through endless, identical hallways, the sound of his footsteps always just behind her. She often wakes up in a cold sweat, her heart pounding against her ribs, convinced she can hear the floorboards creaking outside her bedroom door. She will lie awake for hours, listening, waiting for a threat that is no longer there but feels ever-present, a ghost living inside her own nervous system.
